# Hotjar vs OpenReplay (2026)

## Overview
Hotjar and OpenReplay are two popular tools used for session recording, heatmaps, and user feedback. Both tools help product managers, UX designers, and marketers understand user behavior and identify areas for improvement. The core use case for these tools is to gain insights into how users interact with a website or application, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data or to reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Hotjar offers a free plan with limited features, while OpenReplay is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: OpenReplay allows users to retain full ownership of their data, while Hotjar stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Hotjar is generally easier to set up, with a simpler installation process, while OpenReplay requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: OpenReplay is designed to handle large volumes of traffic and can be scaled horizontally, while Hotjar has limitations on its free plan.
* Integration: OpenReplay has a more extensive API and supports custom integrations, while Hotjar has a more limited set of pre-built integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Hotjar | OpenReplay |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $32-$80+/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | Approximately $32-$80/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | Approximately $160-$320/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Hotjar
* Easy to set up and use
* Offers a free plan with limited features
* Has a user-friendly interface
* Supports heatmaps and user feedback
* Limited control over data storage and ownership
### OpenReplay
* Free and self-hosted
* Offers full control over data ownership and storage
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Supports custom integrations
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain

## When to Choose Each
Hotjar is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who need a simple and easy-to-use tool for session recording and heatmaps. It's also a good option for teams who don't require full control over their data and are willing to pay for a proprietary solution. OpenReplay, on the other hand, is a good choice for larger teams or organizations that require full control over their data and are willing to invest in a self-hosted solution. It's also a good option for teams who need a high degree of customization and extensibility.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Hotjar in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up an OpenReplay instance on your own server or use a cloud provider.
3. Use the OpenReplay API to import your data from Hotjar.
4. Configure your OpenReplay instance to match your Hotjar setup.
5. Test and verify that your data has been migrated correctly.

## Our Take
OpenReplay is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that OpenReplay requires a significant amount of server resources to handle large volumes of traffic. However, for teams who require full control over their data and are willing to invest in a self-hosted solution, OpenReplay is a good choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams who need full control over their data and are willing to invest in a self-hosted solution
* Medium-sized teams who require a high degree of customization and extensibility
* Large teams who need to handle large volumes of traffic and require a scalable solution
* Teams who don't need heatmaps or user feedback features
* Teams who are currently using Hotjar's free plan and need more features

## FAQ
### What is the main difference between Hotjar and OpenReplay?
The main difference is that OpenReplay is free and self-hosted, while Hotjar is a proprietary solution with a free plan and paid upgrades.
### Can I use OpenReplay with my existing Hotjar setup?
Yes, you can export your data from Hotjar and import it into OpenReplay using the API.
### Is OpenReplay suitable for small teams?
Yes, OpenReplay is suitable for small teams who need full control over their data and are willing to invest in a self-hosted solution.
### Does OpenReplay support heatmaps and user feedback?
Yes, OpenReplay supports heatmaps and user feedback, as well as other features such as session recording and custom integrations.
### Is OpenReplay production-ready?
No, OpenReplay is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and maintain.

# Canva vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Canva and Penpot are graphic design platforms used for creating visual content, with Canva being a popular choice for individuals and teams, and Penpot offering a free and open-source alternative. The core use case for both tools is to create and edit designs, and someone would switch from Canva to Penpot for greater control over their data and design files. This comparison is beneficial for teams and individuals looking for a cost-effective and customizable design solution.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Canva offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $15/user/month, while Penpot is completely free.
* Data ownership: Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their data, whereas Canva stores user data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Canva has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Canva has better scalability for large teams, while Penpot's scalability depends on the user's self-hosting capabilities.
* Feature difference: Canva has a more extensive library of templates and design assets, while Penpot has a more customizable and extensible architecture.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Canva | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $15-$30/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $15/user/month * 50 = $750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $15/user/month * 200 = $3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Canva:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large library of templates and design assets
* Collaborative features for teams
* Integrates with other design tools
* Limited control over data and design files
**Penpot:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting available for full data control
* Customizable and extensible architecture
* Community-driven development
* Limited templates and design assets compared to Canva
* Requires technical expertise for self-hosting

## When to Choose Each
Canva is suitable for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who need a straightforward design solution with a wide range of templates and design assets. It's ideal for those who prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over their data and design files. On the other hand, Penpot is suitable for larger teams or organizations that require a high degree of customization and control over their design files. It's also ideal for those who value data sovereignty and are willing to invest time and resources into self-hosting and customizing the platform.

## Migration Path
1. Export your designs from Canva in PNG or PDF format.
2. Set up a Penpot instance on your own server or use a cloud hosting service.
3. Use the Penpot import tool to upload your designs and start editing.
4. Customize Penpot's interface and features to fit your team's needs.
5. Invite your team members to join and collaborate on designs using Penpot.

## Our Take
Penpot is still developing and may not be production-ready for most users, especially those who rely on a wide range of templates and design assets. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's self-hosting capabilities require a significant amount of technical expertise. However, for teams and individuals who value data sovereignty and customization, Penpot is a viable alternative to Canva, and we recommend switching to Penpot if you have the technical resources to support self-hosting and customization.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of 2-5 users who don't need a wide range of templates and design assets
* Individuals who value data sovereignty and are willing to self-host
* Organizations with 10-20 users who require a high degree of customization
* Teams who already have experience with self-hosting and customizing design platforms
* Solo designers who want full control over their design files and don't need collaborative features

## FAQ
### Is Penpot completely free?
Yes, Penpot is completely free and open-source, with no costs per user.
### Can I self-host Penpot?
Yes, Penpot offers self-hosting capabilities, allowing you to have full control over your data and design files.
### Is Penpot as easy to use as Canva?
No, Penpot requires more technical expertise, especially for self-hosting and customization.
### Can I import my Canva designs into Penpot?
Yes, Penpot offers an import tool that allows you to upload your designs from Canva and start editing.
### Is Penpot suitable for large teams?
Not yet, Penpot's scalability depends on the user's self-hosting capabilities, and it may not be suitable for very large teams.

# Canva vs Inkscape (2026)

## Overview
Canva and Inkscape are two popular graphic design tools used for creating visual content. Both tools cater to individuals and teams looking to produce professional-grade designs, with the core use case being the creation of graphics, logos, and other visual elements. The key reason someone would switch from Canva to Inkscape is to gain more control over their design files and hosting, especially for teams with specific data ownership and scalability requirements.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Canva offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $15-$30 per user per month, while Inkscape is completely free.
* Data Ownership: Canva stores design files on its servers, while Inkscape allows users to store files locally or self-host.
* Setup Complexity: Canva has a more user-friendly interface and easier setup, while Inkscape requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: Inkscape is more scalable for large teams and organizations due to its self-hosting option.
* Feature Difference: Canva has a built-in photo editor, while Inkscape relies on external tools for photo editing.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Canva | Inkscape |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $15-$30/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $750-$1500 per month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $3000-$6000 per month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Canva:**
* User-friendly interface
* Wide range of templates and design assets
* Collaborative features
* Integrates with other design tools
* Limited control over design files and hosting
**Inkscape:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option
* High level of customizability
* Steeper learning curve
* Limited photo editing capabilities

## When to Choose Each
Canva is suitable for small to medium-sized teams and individuals who prioritize ease of use and a wide range of design templates. It's ideal for those who don't require advanced customizability or self-hosting. Inkscape, on the other hand, is better suited for large teams and organizations that require more control over their design files and hosting. It's also a good choice for those who are comfortable with a steeper learning curve and require advanced customizability.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Canva design files in SVG format.
2. Download and install Inkscape on your local machine or set up a self-hosted server.
3. Import your SVG files into Inkscape using the built-in import tool.
4. Familiarize yourself with Inkscape's interface and features.
5. Consider seeking additional training or resources to get the most out of Inkscape's advanced features.

## Our Take
Inkscape is not yet production-ready for most users due to its steep learning curve and limited user support. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Inkscape's performance can be slow with complex designs or large files. However, for teams that require advanced customizability and self-hosting, Inkscape is a clear winner. We recommend switching to Inkscape if you're a large team or organization with specific data ownership and scalability requirements, but not if you're an individual or small team that prioritizes ease of use.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (50+ users) that require self-hosting and advanced customizability
* Organizations with strict data ownership and security requirements
* Designers who don't need Canva's built-in photo editor
* Teams that require advanced scalability and performance
* Users who prioritize open-source and free software

## FAQ
### Is Inkscape completely free?
Yes, Inkscape is completely free and open-source. It has no paid plans or licensing fees.
### Can I use Inkscape for photo editing?
Inkscape is not ideal for photo editing, as it's primarily a vector graphics editor. You may need to use external tools for photo editing.
### Is Canva suitable for large teams?
Canva can be suitable for large teams, but it may become expensive and limiting in terms of data ownership and scalability.
### Can I self-host Canva?
No, Canva does not offer self-hosting options. You must use their cloud-based service.
### Is Inkscape compatible with Canva files?
Yes, Inkscape can import SVG files exported from Canva. However, some features or formatting may not be preserved.

# Adobe Illustrator vs Inkscape

## Overview

Industry-standard vector graphics editor. is a popular proprietary tool in the design space. Inkscape is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Adobe Illustrator costs $20.99-$54.99/month; Inkscape is Free
- **License**: Adobe Illustrator is Proprietary; Inkscape is GPL 3.0
- **Data ownership**: Inkscape can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Inkscape eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Inkscape has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Adobe Illustrator | Inkscape |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $20.99-$54.99/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$1,050/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$4,198/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Adobe Illustrator

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Inkscape

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [inkscape/inkscape](https://github.com/inkscape/inkscape) * ~4k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Adobe Illustrator if:** Adobe Illustrator is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Inkscape if:** Inkscape is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Adobe Illustrator in its standard export format, review Inkscape import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Inkscape is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Adobe Illustrator tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Inkscape instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Adobe Illustrator, switching to self-hosted Inkscape will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Adobe Illustrator until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Adobe Illustrator paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

Yes. Inkscape is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Adobe Illustrator to Inkscape?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Adobe Illustrator data, follow the Inkscape import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Inkscape get regular updates?
Yes. Inkscape has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Inkscape without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

# Adobe Premiere Pro vs Kdenlive (2026)

## Overview
Adobe Premiere Pro and Kdenlive are two video editing tools used for post-production and video creation. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from a paid, proprietary solution to a free, open-source alternative, with the core use case being professional video editing. The key reason someone would switch is to reduce costs and gain more control over their data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Adobe Premiere Pro requires a monthly subscription, while Kdenlive is free to use.
* Data Ownership: Adobe Premiere Pro stores project files in a proprietary format, whereas Kdenlive uses an open standard.
* Setup Complexity: Adobe Premiere Pro has a more streamlined setup process, while Kdenlive requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Adobe Premiere Pro is designed for large-scale productions and has better support for collaborative workflows, whereas Kdenlive is more suited for individual creators or small teams.
* Multi-camera editing: Adobe Premiere Pro has more advanced multi-camera editing features, including automatic syncing and editing tools, whereas Kdenlive's multi-camera editing capabilities are more basic.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Adobe Premiere Pro | Kdenlive |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $20.99-$54.99/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $1049.50-$2749.50/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $4198-$10,998.80/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Adobe Premiere Pro:**
* Advanced multi-camera editing features
* Better support for collaborative workflows
* More extensive library of plugins and integrations
* Streamlined setup process
* Industry-standard for professional video editing
**Kdenlive:**
* Free to use
* Open-source and community-driven
* Self-hosting available
* Cross-platform compatibility
* Limited support for advanced collaborative workflows

## When to Choose Each
Adobe Premiere Pro is the better choice for large-scale productions, collaborative teams, and those who require advanced multi-camera editing features. It is also the industry standard for professional video editing, making it easier to find trained professionals and integrate with other tools. Kdenlive, on the other hand, is suitable for individual creators, small teams, or those on a tight budget. It is also a good choice for those who value data ownership and control, as well as those who prefer a self-hosted solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Adobe Premiere Pro project as an EDL (Edit Decision List) file.
2. Import the EDL file into Kdenlive using the "Import" tool.
3. Re-link your media files to their new locations, as Kdenlive may not be able to find the original files.
4. Re-apply any effects or color grading that were not preserved during the import process.
5. Test and refine your project to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Kdenlive is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the advanced features and polish of Adobe Premiere Pro. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Kdenlive's multi-camera editing features are not as advanced as those in Adobe Premiere Pro. However, for individual creators or small teams who do not require these advanced features, Kdenlive is a viable alternative that can save them a significant amount of money.

## Who Should Switch
* Solo video creators who do not need advanced collaborative features
* Small teams of 2-5 people who can manage their own workflow
* Budget-conscious creators who prioritize cost savings over advanced features
* Educational institutions or non-profits who need a free or low-cost video editing solution
* Developers who want to integrate a video editing tool into their own application

## FAQ
### Can I use Kdenlive for commercial projects?
Yes, Kdenlive is free to use for commercial projects, and its GPL 2.0 license does not impose any restrictions on commercial use.
### Is Kdenlive available for Windows?
Yes, Kdenlive is available for Windows, as well as Linux and macOS.
### Can I import Adobe Premiere Pro projects into Kdenlive?
Yes, Kdenlive can import Adobe Premiere Pro projects via the EDL file format, but some features may not be preserved.
### Does Kdenlive support 4K video editing?
Yes, Kdenlive supports 4K video editing, as well as other high-resolution formats.
### Is Kdenlive suitable for large-scale productions?
No, Kdenlive is not yet suitable for large-scale productions that require advanced collaborative features and multi-camera editing.

Web design and prototyping tool with advanced animations. is a popular proprietary tool in the design space. Plasmic is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

- **Cost**: Framer costs Free / $15-$35/month; Plasmic is Free (self-hosted)

- **Data ownership**: Plasmic can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Plasmic eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Plasmic has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|

## Pros and Cons

### Framer

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Plasmic

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [plasmicapp/plasmic](https://github.com/plasmicapp/plasmic) * ~4k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Framer if:** Framer is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Plasmic if:** Plasmic is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

## Our Take

Plasmic is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Framer tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Plasmic instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

# Figma vs Inkscape (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Inkscape are two popular design tools used for creating and editing vector graphics. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from a proprietary platform to an open-source alternative or vice versa, with the core use case being vector graphic design and the key reason to switch being data ownership and cost.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Inkscape is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Figma stores designs on its proprietary servers, while Inkscape allows users to store designs locally or on self-hosted servers.
* Setup Complexity: Figma has a more straightforward setup process, while Inkscape requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Figma is more scalable and can handle large teams and complex designs, while Inkscape may struggle with very large files and teams.
* Feature Difference: Figma has a more comprehensive collaboration feature set, including real-time commenting and @mentions, while Inkscape relies on external tools for collaboration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Inkscape |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Pros:
	+ Easy to use and set up
	+ Comprehensive collaboration features
	+ Large community and plenty of resources
	+ Scalable and performant
	+ Integrates well with other design tools
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Limited control over data storage and ownership
	+ Limited customization options
### Inkscape
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Highly customizable
	+ Cross-platform compatibility
	+ Plenty of features for vector graphic design
	+ Self-hosting options
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve
	+ Limited collaboration features
	+ May struggle with large files and teams
	+ Not as polished as Figma

## When to Choose Each
Figma is the better choice for large teams and enterprises that require a scalable and collaborative design solution. It's also a good fit for teams that are already invested in the Figma ecosystem and don't mind the cost. Inkscape, on the other hand, is a better choice for individuals, small teams, and organizations that value data ownership and customization. It's also a good fit for teams that are on a tight budget and don't require advanced collaboration features.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs as SVG files.
2. Install Inkscape on your local machine or set up a self-hosted server.
3. Import the SVG files into Inkscape using the "File" > "Import" menu.
4. Adjust the design settings and layout to fit Inkscape's interface and features.
5. Use Inkscape's built-in features and extensions to enhance and customize your designs.

## Our Take
Inkscape is not yet production-ready for most users, especially those who rely on advanced collaboration features and scalability. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Inkscape's performance can degrade with very large files and complex designs. However, for individuals and small teams that value data ownership and customization, Inkscape is a great alternative to Figma, and we recommend switching to Inkscape if you don't require advanced collaboration features and are comfortable with a steeper learning curve.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't require advanced collaboration features
* Individuals who value data ownership and customization
* Organizations on a tight budget that don't mind a steeper learning curve
* Teams that primarily work with vector graphics and don't require advanced raster editing features
* Educational institutions that want to teach design principles without breaking the bank

## FAQ
### Is Inkscape free?
Yes, Inkscape is completely free and open-source.
### Can I use Inkscape for collaboration?
Inkscape has limited collaboration features, but you can use external tools to enhance collaboration.
### Is Figma self-hosted?
No, Figma is not available for self-hosting.
### Can I import Figma designs into Inkscape?
Yes, you can import Figma designs into Inkscape using the SVG file format.
### Is Inkscape available for Windows, Mac, and Linux?
Yes, Inkscape is available for all three platforms.
